sections.heading: Uttar Pradesh- Monument- Bara Imambara, Lucknow
sections.content: Asaf-ud-Daulah, an enthusiastic builder of monuments shifted his capital to Lucknow from Faizabad. Driven with an ambition to testify his architectural zeal, the Bara Imambara was built by this generous Nawab, who employed more than 22,000 people, including nobles. He adopted a dual policy of construction. During the day, the Imambara was built, and at night, the workers destroyed parts of what had been built. This was to ensure that no one remained unemployed, and the edifice was not completed too soon. This is indeed a monumental feat considering the fact that it was once the largest vaulted hall in the world, with a 50 feet high roof, spanning an area of 162 feet. The galleries and corridors within the great Imambara form a complicated and intricate labyrinth (bhool-bhuliaya) through which at times it is difficult to find ones way.

sections.heading: Uttar Pradesh- Monument- Rumi Darwaza
sections.content: Towards the west of the Imambara is the Rumi Darwaza or the Turkish Gate built. The 60 feet high gateway stands as an equally grand entrance to the great hall. During the Nawabi era, it is believed that a huge lantern placed atop the Rumi Darwaza would light up the pathway, while jets of water gushed from the numerous fountains created on the rim of the gateway.

sections.heading: Qaiser Bagh Palace
sections.content: flanked by two mermaid gates (Lakkhi gate) at eastern and western ends. On the right end was Chandiwali Baradari, which it is believed was paved with sliver and the Khas Muqam and Badshah Manzil, were the special residences of the king. During the days of the mutiny Begum Hazrat Mahal held court from here. The buildings at the Qaiser Bagh quadrangle were occupied chiefly by ladies of the Harem. One of his favourite wives Nawab Mashuq Mahal used to live in it.

sections.heading: Uttar Pradesh- Monument- Residency
sections.content: Asaf-ud-Daulas brother Sadat Ali proved to be a great builder who introduced a large number of architectural styles. One of his best-known monuments is the Residency, which was built for the British Residents. The ruins of the Residency stand desolate as a mute witness to the Mutiny of 1857 when it was almost completely destroyed. The redbrick ruins and the shattered walls are still scarred by cannon shots. The cemetery at the nearby ruined church has the graves of 2000 men, women and children. The 1857 Memorial Museum at the Residency has been established and designed to present a visual accounts of the freedom struggle of 1857. Located in a portion which was annex of the main Residency building, original photographs and lithographs of many sites, connected with the uprising, and paintings depicting significant events of the uprising have been displayed along with portraits of local heroes. Period objects such as guns, swords, shields, cannons, rank badges, medals and other items also form part of the display.

sections.heading: Uttar Pradesh- Monument- Chhota Imambara
sections.content: The British crowned the third king of Awadh, Muhammad Ali in 1837 at a ripe old age of 63. He was a just and popular ruler under whom Lucknow once again regained its splendor for a brief spell. Interested in building activities, he built his own Imambara as well as the Juma Masjid. The Chhota Imambara as it had been called later was left incomplete by Muhammad Ali, was later completed by Begum Mallika Jehan of the Royal family. It has a golden dome, exquisite chandeliers, huge mirrors, silver minbar, colourful interiors and delicate calligraphy on its arched entrance.

sections.heading: Uttar Pradesh- Introduction- Allahabad
sections.content: Prayag, now known as Allahabad is one of the most famous ancient pilgrimage  being worshipped for Sangam  the confluence of the three holy rivers  Ganga, Yamuna and Saraswati.

sections.heading: Uttar Pradesh- Fairs & Festivals- Kumbh
sections.content: Every year in the month of January and February, this ancient city vibrates when thousands of devotees from all over the world come for the holy dip at Sangam  called Kumbh. Every 12 years there is Maha Kumbh and every 6 years Ardh Kumbh takes place.

sections.heading: Uttar Pradesh- Fairs & Festivals- Magh Mela
sections.content: The Magh Mela is held annually, in January and February that lasts for 15 days. The Mela (fair), according to the mythology commemorates the struggle between Gods and demons over a kumbh (pot) of amrit, the elixir of life. When the amrit surfaced from the bottom of the ocean, Lord Vishnu, Preserver of the Universe ran away with the pot of amrit. While he was running, four drops of the elixir fell on the sites that are now the holy towns of Allahabad, Haridwar, Nasik and Ujjain.

sections.heading: Uttar Pradesh- Introduction- Mathura
sections.content: Mathura, the birthplace of Lord Krishna was known as Brij Bhoomi. Mathura is surrounded by numerous sites which have been associated with Lord Krishna. Vrindavan was the place where He spent his childhood with cowherds, and gopis, or the village maidens is located a few kms from Mathura. This region has hundreds of small and big temples which attract pilgrims throughtout the year. Some of the significant temples are, Dwarikadeesh temple, the temple at Krishna Janmbhoomi, Shri Radha Raman temple, Shri Govind Dev temple etc.

sections.heading: Mathura Museum
sections.content: The Mathura school of sculpture known for the Mathura style flourished here for almost 1200 Years. Starting from the Kushan period around 100 BCE and reaching its peak during the Gupta period (AD 325 to 600). The sculptures made in red sandstone were marked by sharp and beautiful features, graceful and slim body, with many folds of transparent drapery and a new style of coiffure. The collection of Mathura sculptures and terracottas are displayed in the Government Museum at Mathura. Established in 1874, the Mathura Museum is of great importance among the museums in India. Exhibiting a rich collection of sculptures belonging to the Mathura School including sculptures dating back to the second century BCE, graceful statues of Buddha and exquisitely carved female figures in addition to images of deities, excellent collection of Buddhist, Brahminical and Jain sculptures in ancient red sandstone it has earned worldwide acclaim. Perhaps the most impressive work of art displayed here is the headless life-size statue of Kanishka. The Mathura school of art adopted the traditions of the early Indian art of Bharhut and Sanchi . Starting with the earliest terracotta figures of the mother goddess, the free use of elaborate motifs in hairstyles and drapes, and the fusion of the old Indian -cults as the worship of yakshas are all important features of this school of art.

sections.heading: Uttar Pradesh- Fairs & Festivals- Holi/ Janamashtami
sections.content: Holi and Janamashtami are two festivals celebrated with great fervour in Mathura. Both these festivals are associated with Lord Krishna and in Holi, festivities start by offering colours to the Lord at the temples before it is celebrated on the streets. Artists from various parts of the country gather here to perform raas leela, or divine dance recitals of Krishnas by devotees. Gayan mandalis, or singing troupes that render folk songs particularly associated with Holi, flock to this place. Janamashtami too is celebrated on the day when Krishna was born. Idols of Krishna and Radha are decorated beautifully and then worshipped.

sections.heading: Uttar Pradesh- Introduction- Agra
sections.content: Agra, the city of architectural wonders is more than just a decadent city of graveyards and stones. It is a vibrant centre of culture, art and religious philosophies. Agra is one of the richest heritage sites in India with numerous amazing Mughal monuments from the magnificent Taj Mahal to sober tombs likeAkbar's mausoleum at Sikandra. Agra is an architect's and historian's delight. The impressive Agra fort, the tombs of Mughal royalty, formal Mughal gardens and the fabulous city of Fatehpur Sikri near Agra are historic sites having unique architectural features and represent the best examples of Mughal architecture in India.

sections.heading: Uttar Pradesh- Monument- Tomb of Itmad-ud-Daula
sections.content: Tomb of Itmad-ud-Daula is one of the most attractive structures in Agra. Designed by Nur Jahan the favorite queen of Jahangir, for her father, the structure is renowned for its pietra dura decoration i.e. the inlaid stonework and the carvings. It is the first Mughal building to be constructed of white inlaid marble, a type of architecture which becomes characteristic of Mughal buildings in the seventeenth century. Believed to have inspired the design of the Taj Mahal, the tomb stands on a low platform and is rectangular with four minars or domed towers growing out of its four corners. The roof is flat, and at the centre is a small roofed pavilion. The marble façade is inlaid with patterns in multi-coloured stones and colourful intarsia representations of vases with flowers, wine cups, cypresses and fruit trees, while much of the second storey is composed of exquisitely carved pierced screens.The structure is set within a formal charbagh and is approached by a monumental gate.

sections.heading: Uttar Pradesh- Agra- Monument- Taj Mahal
sections.content: Overlooking the River Yamuna, the Taj Mahal was built by Emperor Shah Jahan to enshrine the body of his favourite wife, Arjumand Banu Begum, better known as Mumtaz Mahal who died shortly after giving birth to her fourteenth child, in 1631. The layout follows a distinctly Islamic theme representing Paradise. The walled complex is approached from the south through a massive arched gateway topped with delicate domes and adorned with Koranic verses, directly aligned with the Taj. Ustad Isa of Turkey is credited to have been the main architect along with Ismail Afandi, who built the domes. Chiranji Lal was called from Delhi to pattern the mosaic while Amanat Khan was the master calligrapher from Persia. Stone cutters came all the way from Baluchistan. Square in shape, the Taj Mahal known for its symmetry, sits on a raised platform surrounded by four minarets. The fully developed four minarets mark an important stage in Mughal architecture. The most remarkable feature of these minarets is their harmony with the tomb. The Taj surmounts a square marble platform marked at each corner by a high minaret. It is topped with a huge central dome , a bulging white double - dome with a broad padma-kosa (lotus - petals) and beautiful Kalasa-finial mounted on the tomb, capped by a crowning brass spire. It is embellished with extraordinarily fine detail of relief carving, highlighted by floral patterns of precious stones. Carved vases of flowers including roses, tulips and narcissi, rise subtly out of the marble base, a pattern repeated more colourfully and inlaid with precious stones around the four great arched recesses on each side. Chhatris flank the dome on all the four angles which appear to be attached to the dome when viewed from all sides. At the Taj the builder calculated the distance between the two features for the precise relationship they were intended to present together. The plan, which is also known as panch-ratna gives the Taj Mahal such a remarkable, impressive and unparalleled grace. The marble mausoleum is square in plan with chamfered corners. Each facade of the tomb is composed of a grand iwan framed by bands of calligraphy. The doorways inside these iwans are also adorned with calligraphy and is flanked on both sides by small double arches one over the other. Each section in the facade is crowned by beautiful pinnacles with lotus buds and finials. The 99 names of Allah adorn the top of Mumtaz's tomb, and set into Shah Jahan's is a pen box, the hallmark of a male ruler. These cenotaphs, in accordance with Moghul tradition, are only representations of the real coffins, which lie in the same positions in an unadorned and humid crypt below. The pietra dura or inlay has been very well combined with the jali-work. The inlay work on the spandrels of the arches in the interior and exterior add magnificence to the overall aesthetic effect. Bouquets of flowers, zigzag motifs and series of small arches are some of the most commonly used decorative elements. Slender twigs, twisting leaves and bold flowers combine to give the monument a beautiful look. Contemporary texts specify the stones used in decoration and inlay work they are- Lapis lazuli, various types of jasper, agate, carnelian, jade, amethyst, turquoise, onyx, coral etc. The Makrana marble with its pearly clarity has contributed most to the beauty of the Taj Mahal. A number of marks are engraved on red stone slabs, on the pathways, stairs, plinths and pavements of the Taj Mahal. Some of them are- symbolic motifs swastika, chakra, aako, a (Hexagon), Paucako,a (Pentagon), aakh (conch-shell), animated motifs - fish, bird, geometrical motifs - triangle, square, rectangle, floral motifs- leaves and petals of the flowers chiefly lotus. The Taj stands at the end of superb gardens designed in the charbagh style so popular among the Persian architects. Divided into four quadrants by waterways, they evoke the Islamic image of the Gardens of Paradise, as according to the holy Koran, a garden is symbolic of paradise where rivers flow with water, milk, wine and honey. The "rivers" converge at a marble tank in the centre that corresponds to al-Kawthar, the celestial pool of abundance mentioned in the Koran. Another genius of the architect is reflected in the layout of the fountains and somber rows of cypress trees, which are present only on the north-south water canal, lest the attention of the onlooker would be diverted to the sides.

sections.heading: Agra Fort
sections.content: Built by the Mughal emperor Akbar, the Agra fort contains numerous impressive structures like the Jahangir Mahal, Khas Mahal, Diwan-i-Khass, Diwan-i-Am, Machchhi Bhawan and Moti Masjid. Imprisoned in the Agra fort by his son Aurangzeb, Shah Jahan spent his last days in the Musamman Burj of the Agra fort. The Musamman Burj is located on the left of the Khaas Mahal. It is a beautiful octagonal tower with an open pavilion. The Jahangiri Mahal was built by Akbar and is one of the few structures that survives from his reign. It is a stately building with rows of ornate pillars with elaborate hanging brackets set around an open courtyard. One of the most beautiful complexes in the fort is the Khaas Mahal constructed by Shahjahan. The central area has a marble courtyard, a rectangular pool with frilled edges and a fountain. The Diwan-e-Khas boasts of Shahjahans evolved and mature style, with cusped arches and rich lattice marble screens and veneers.

sections.heading: Uttar Pradesh- Monument- Fatehpur Sikri
sections.content: Fatehpur Sikri was a planned town by Akbar with great care and planning in the honor of Sheikh Salim Chisti but had to be abandoned only after fifteen years due to scarcity of water in the town. Sheikh Salim Chishti was a Sufi saint who blessed the Akbar with his first son and heir, who was named Salim after him and later came to be known as Jehangir. The town was originally named Sikri after the village, where it was founded but its twin city Fatehpur (Victory Town) was erected to celebrate Akbar's conquest of Gujarat. This complex includes Jodha Bai's palace, Hawa Mahal, Birbal's House, Stables, Panch Mahal, Mariyam's House, Zenana Garden, Nagina Masjid, and the Imperial Harem. This was the private place for the women of the palace. This place was designed keeping in mind the purdah custom for women; still the place is well lighted and well ventilated. Buland Darwaza at Fatehpur Sikri was built by Akbar to commemorate his victory over Gujarat. Made of red and buff sandstone, decorated by carving and inlaying of white and black marble and approached by 42 steps it is the highest gateway in the world and an astounding example of the Mughal architecture. Jami Masjid, one of the most elegant and sacred building is situated on the highest point of the ridge where Fatehpur Sikri is situated. The Tomb of the famous Sufi saint Sheikh Salim Chishti are a part of this spacious mosque complex. Built in the supervision of the saint himself and his descendants, it was completed in 1571. The vast quadrangle has the mosque on the western side. The main rectangular mosque consists of a central nave with a single dome, two colonnaded halls on its either side with two square chambers crowned with dome. The elegant and beautifully carved mehrabs adorn the main chamber and the two smaller rooms. The mosque marks the phase of transition in Islamic art as the indigenous architectural elements were blended with the Persian architecture. The pillared dalan of the facade, the iwan with three arched openings also framed by panels and crowned by five chhatris and the central mehrab adorned with inlaid mosaic of stones that are bordered by glazed tiles and has golden inscriptions on royal blue background. The interiors of the iwan are adorned with watercolor paintings depicting stylized floral designs. Even the dado panels, spandrels of arch, squinches and soffits are also painted profusely. Unlike other monuments, where domes are supported on squinches, here elegant corbelled pendentives support the dome. Tansen's Baradari Known as 'Barahdari' as it has twelve doorways, this single-storeyed red sandstone building is rectangular in shape with three doorways on each side. The arched doorways grace its northern and southern sides while the eastern and western sides have flat-roofed doorways. Though, people believe that Tansen, one of the Nine Gems of Akbar's court who was a famous musician lived here, the idea seems to be too absurd to be true. Not only the building is too small for a nobleman's house with only a single oblong hall, it has no attachments that are a must in a residential house such as hammams or baths, toilets or room for the ladies. Akbar's court had Navratnas or Nine Jewels, a term denoting a group of nine extraordinary people who have since become a part of Akbar's legend. They were: Birbal who was a brilliant administrator famous for his great wit and justness. Bhagwant Das, the Commander-in-Chief of the Mughal Armies. Man Singh, one of Akbar's most trusted Generals. Todar Mal, the empire's Finance minister. Tansen, beloved court singer of Akbar. Abul Fazl, the official State Historian of Akbar's reign and author of Akbarnama, the court chronicle of the Emperor Akbar. Abdul Rahim Khanikhana, a renowned poet in Persian, Sanskrit, and Hindustani. Aziaodin, a sage and one of the chief advisors of the Emperor, along with the other Navratnas. Poet Faizi who is best known for his Nal u Daman, a poetic rendering of the Sanskrit story of Nala and Damayanti.

sections.heading: Uttar Pradesh- Monument- Fatehpur Sikri
sections.content: Birbal's house stands near the northwest corner of JodhaBai's palace. It is one of the marvelous buildings of Imperial Harem. It consists of four square rooms, each are interconnected through open doorways and two oblong entrance porches. While all four rooms, have flat ceilings, porches have triangular ceiling with pyramidal roofs. Shafts of these pilasters have been divided into three zones, which contain three different kind of decoration like single border designs, arabesque geometrical designs and stylized floral designs. An extension of northern suite of Jodha Bai's palace, Hawa Mahal is composed of beautiful jali screens. Therefore, it is named as Hawa Mahal or Palace of Breeze. This kind of arrangement of screens keeps the interior cool and at the same time ensured purdah for ladies. The purpose of Viaduct passage was to allow the ladies of the imperial Harem to go on outings in purdah. This has been provided from west of the Hawa Mahal to the plain below. It was originally closed with beautiful stone screens and extended upto Hathi Pol and Sangin Burj, but now only a part of it is survived. Several Hindu motifs like hans (swan), parrot, elephants, lotus, srivatsa mark, ghantmala etc. are decorated in the interior The colonnaded dalan contains curvilinear square pillars with beautiful moldings and extremely graceful brackets. The western suite, which serves the purpose of temple, contains beautiful curvilinear pillars with brackets. This suite contains vedikas and the super structure of the building comprises of chhatris, semi-circular domes and triangular tiled roofs which bear traces of arabesque designs in glazed tiles. Panch Mahal, a five-floored pillared pavilion is an extraordinary building was called badgir or wind tower, which was constructed to alleviate the heat and is a very popular architectural mechanism of Persian architecture. The first floor has 84 pillars with each row of eight pillars arranged in north to south direction and six pillars arranged in east to west direction. The second floor has 56 pillars beautiful carved pillars with unique designs with row of six pillars in north to south direction and row of four pillars in east to west direction and also. Capitals of these pillars also contain beautiful carved designs like floral vase, arch or rosette pattern.

sections.heading: Uttar Pradesh- Introduction- Varanasi
sections.content: The land of Varanasi (Kashi) has been the ultimate pilgrimage spot for Hindus for ages. Often referred to as Benares, Varanasi is the oldest living city in the world. Varanasi has also been a great center of learning for ages and is associated with spiritualism, mysticism, Sanskrit, yoga and honored authors such as the ever-famous novelist Prem Chand and Tulsi Das, the famous saint-poet who wrote RamCharit Manas.

sections.heading: Uttar Pradesh- Monument- Ghats of Varanasi
sections.content: With more than 100 ghats along the Ganga some of the prominent and popular Ghats at Varanasi are the Dasaswamedh Ghat, Manikarnika Ghat, Harischandra Ghat, Kabir Ghat and Assi Ghat. Dasaswamedh Ghat is one of the most important Ghats of Varanasi. Dasaswamedh literally means the river front of ten sacrificed horses where ten times the Ashwamedha Yagya has been performed by different kings. Manikarnika Ghat is the main cremation ghat of Varanasi. Manikarnika Ghat is one of the oldest and most sacred ghats in Benaras. Hindus believe that who ever is being cremated here after the death becomes free from the cycle of births. Tulsi Ghat is named after the great Hindu poet of the sixteenth century, Tulsidas, who composed the, Ramcharitmanas sitting at this ghat in Varanasi. Perhaps, to commemorate this, a temple of Lord Rama was built on the Tulsi Ghat. Many of the relics of Tulsisas are preserved at the Tulsi Ghat. The house in which Tulsidas died has been preserved and his samadhi, wooden clogs, pillow and the idol of Hanuman, which Tulsidas worshipped, are all still intact here.

sections.heading: Uttar Pradesh- Performing Art- Ram Lila
sections.content: Ram Lila is a popular enactment of the epic Ramayana. Ram Lila celebration forms an integral part of peoples cultural life. It is believed that the great saint Tulsidas started the tradition of Ram Lila, the enactment of the story of Lord Ram. The Ramcharitamanas, written by him, forms the basis of Ram Lila performances till today. The Ramnagar Ram Lila (at Varanasi) is enacted in the most traditional style. This special Ram Lila of Ramnagar lasts for almost one month. Ram Lila of Ramnagar was started in the first quarter of the nineteenth century by the then Maharaja of Benaras, Udit Narayan Singh. Hundreds of Sadhus called the 'Ramayanis' come to watch and recite the Ramayana. The uniqueness of this Ram Lila is that it is not enacted on the stage but different events from the life of Lord Rama takes place at different localesidentified for the performance on different days. Thus, we have Ashok Vatika, Lanka etc at different locations in the town. The audience moves along with the performers with every episode, to the next location. The most amazing thing about the Ram Lila of Ramnagar is its sober character. It is incredible to see that electric lights, mikes and loudspeakers are hardly used in the performances, even when the audience number in thousands.

sections.heading: UttarPradesh- Monument- Sarnath
sections.content: About 10 km from the holy city of Varanasi, is the Sarnath where Buddha delivered his first sermon after gaining enlightenment. The mantra, Buddham Sharanam Gachhami, owes its origin to Sarnath. On the day before his death Buddha included Sarnath along with Lumbini, Bodh Gaya and Kushinagar as the four places he thought to be sacred to his followers. It makes Sarnath one of the most venerated Buddhist places. Besides Buddhism, Sarnath is also connected with Jainism. Some of the important Buddhist monuments at Sarnath are the Dhamekha stupa, the Chaukhandi stupa and monasteries and temples of different schools of Buddhism from Japan, China, Thailand, Burma etc. The Indian Buddhist society called Mahabodhi Society maintains a deer park around the Buddha temple. The Mahabodhi Temple within the park has a tooth relic of the Buddha. The capital of Ashoka pillar of Sarnath is the national emblem of India. Chaukhandi Stupa is one of the important Buddhist Stupas at Sarnath. It is a lofty mound of brick, whose square edifice is surrounded by an octagonal tower. It was built to mark the place where Lord Buddha met his firstdisciples as he traveled from Bodh Gaya to Sarnath. The Dhamekh Stupa is the most remarkable and massive structure at Sarnath. Built partly in stone and partly in brick, the stone facing the lower part is decorated with delicate floral carvings of Gupta period. Dhamekh Stupa at Sarnath as it signifies the place where Buddha delivered his first sermon.

sections.heading: Uttar Pradesh- Museum- Sarnath Museum
sections.content: Sarnath has yielded a rich collection of sculptures, artifacts and edifices comprising numerous Buddha and Bodhisattva images and other ancient remains. To house all the findings and excavations at Sarnath, the Archaeological Survey of India established a site Museum at Sarnath. Finest specimens of Buddhist art and other important remains have been housed at the museum. While the single most famous exhibit of this museum is the lion capital, the Sarnath museum has a small but awe-inspiring collection of Buddhist artifacts. Among the displays is a beautiful sculpture of the Buddha from the fifth century. The Buddha sits cross-legged, with eyes downcast in deep meditation, and a halo around his head. Also worth exploring are several beautiful figures of the Bodhisattvas. Of other Buddhist remains there is an impressive and amazingly beautiful, life-size standing Bodhisattva and a delicate image of the Bodhisattva with a lotus and yet another bronze sculpture showing the Bodhisattva with multiple arms. The museum at Sarnath also houses an excellent collection of figures and sculptures from the Mauryan, the Kushana and the Gupta periods. Prominent of them is the earliest Buddha image found at Sarnath and many images of Hindu Gods dating from the 9th to 12th centuries.

sections.heading: Sarnath Museum Buddha
sections.content: The Ashoka Lion capital or the Sarnath lion capital is the national symbol of India. The Sarnath pillar bears one of the Edicts of Ashoka, an inscription against division within the Buddhist community, which reads, "No one shall cause division in the order of monks". The Sarnath pillar is a column surmounted by a capital, a canopy representing an inverted bell-shaped lotus flower, which consists of a short cylindrical abacus with four 24-spoked Dharma wheels with four animals (an elephant, a bull, a horse, a lion). The four animals in the Sarnath capital are believed to symbolize different steps of Lord Buddha's life. The Elephant represents the Buddha's idea in reference to the dream of Queen Maya of a white elephant entering her womb. The Bull represents desire during the life of the Buddha as a prince. The Horse represents Buddha's departure from palatial life. The Lion represents the accomplishment of Buddha hood. Besides the religious interpretations, there are some non-religious interpretations also about the symbolism of the Ashoka capital pillar at Sarnath. According to them, the four lions symbolize Ashoka's rule over the four directions, the wheels as symbols of his enlightened rule (Chakravartin) and the four animals as symbols of four adjoining territories of India.

sections.heading: Uttar Pradesh- Monument- Kapilvastu
sections.content: Piprahwa 22 km from Siddharthnagar is identified with ancient Kapilvastu where Lord Buddha spent the early years of his life. Kapilvastu was the capital of the Shakya clan whose ruler was the father of Lord Buddha, and therefore Lord Buddha is also called as Shakyamuni. Prince Gautam, as the Buddha was then known, left his palace in Kapilvastu at the age of 29, and only to come back after 12 years, after attaining enlightenment. Today, Kapilvastu comprises of several villages, mainly Piprahwa and Ganvaria. A large Stupa stands at the ancient site which is said to have housed the bone relics of Lord Buddha. The presence of these relics is testified by an ancient Brahmi inscription found at Piprahwa. The ruins of the royal palace of King Shuddhodhana, the father of Prince Gautam are spread over a large area It was at this place, where the Shakya prince Siddhartha Gautama had spent 29 years of his life before leaving home to become the Buddha.

sections.heading: Uttar Pradesh- Monument- Kapilvastu Stupa Complex
sections.content: This is the main archaeological site which was discovered during excavations. The seals and inscriptions over the lid of the pot discovered read Om Deoputra Vihare Kapilvastu Bhikschu Mahasanghasa and Om Deoputra Vihare Kapilvastu Bhikschu Sanghasa. The title Deoputra refers to Kanishka, a great patron of Buddhism who built the biggest Vihara at Kapilvastu and renovated the main stupa here.

sections.heading: Uttar Pradesh- Monument- Kushinagar
sections.content: Kushinagar, one of the principal centres of the Buddhist pilgrimage, is the place where Lord Buddha attained Maharparinivana  gained freedom from rebirth. The Chinese travelers Fa Hien and Hieun Tsang have also mentioned Kushinagar in their travelogues. The credit for bringing this ancient site to light goes to General A. Cunningham and A.C.L. Carlleyle who, after excavating the site in 1861, established its antiquity for the first time. Later, more

sections.heading: Nirvana temple
sections.content: excavations were conducted by the Archaeological Survey of India at Kushinagar. The monuments of Kushinagar are clustered in threedistinct groups comprising the main site at the Nirvana temple, the central Stupa and surrounding monastery of Mathakuar Kot in the south-west and the Ramabhar Stupa, a kilometer to the east. Nirvana Stupa is a huge brickwork stupa, stands at a height of 2.74 mtr. A copper vessel was unearthed at this site. It bore an inscription in ancient Brahmi, which stated that Lord Buddha's remains had been deposited here. Mahaparinirvana Temple houses a 6.10 meter long statue of the reclining Buddha. Carved from Chunar sandstone, the statue represents the dying Buddha reclining on his right side. An inscription below dates the statue to the fifth century. Mathakuar Shrine a stone image of Lord Buddha in the Bhumi Sparsha Mudra (posture touching the earth while sitting) under the Bodhi tree was excavated here. The inscription at the base of the statue dates it to tenth eleventh century. Adjacent to this shrine, ruins of a monastery have also been discovered. Ramabhar Stupa About 1.5 km away from Mahaparinirvana temple, is a large Stupa rising to a height of 15 meters. It marks the site where Lord Buddha was cremated. In ancient Buddhist texts, this stupa has been referred to as Mukut-Bandhan Chaitya Kushinagar is also known as Kasia or Kusinara. The founder of Buddhism, Lord Buddha passed away at this place near the Hiranyavati River and was cremated at the Ramabhar stupa. It was once a celebrated center of the Malla kingdom. Many of its stupas and viharas date back to 230 BCE-413 CE when its prosperity was at the peak. The Mauryan emperor Ashoka added grandeur to this place by getting the magnificent statue of Buddha carved on a single piece of red sandstone. All the three famous Chinese scholar Fa Hien, Huen Tsang, and I-tsing, travellers to India visited Kushinagar. With the decline of Buddhism, however, Kushinagar lost its importance and suffered much neglect. It was only in the nineteenth century that Cunningham excavated many important remnants of the main site such as the Matha Kuar and Ramabhar stupa. Today, people from all over the world visit Kushinagar. Many national and international societies and groups have established their centers here.

sections.heading: Uttar Pradesh- Monument- Sravasti
sections.content: Sravasti, capital of the ancient Kosala kingdom is sacred to Buddhists because it is here that Lord Buddha performed the greatest of his miracles. These miracles include that of the Buddha creating multiple images of himself, hence forth has been among the favorite themes of Buddhist art. An active centre of Buddhism even in the Buddhas lifetime, the Buddha himself spent many summers here, and delivered important sermons. It was here that Anathapindaka built a large monastery for the reception of the Buddha in the garden of Prince Jeta. Later, several shrines and other monasteries arose at this sacred spot. Sravasti has been identified with the remains at Saheth - Maheth on the borders of the Gonda and Bahraich districts. Srarvasti also is also important for Jain devotees who visit during the month of Kartik (Oct.-Nov.) to commemorate the bithday of Jain Tirthankar Lord Sambhavnath, when an annual fair is held. Saheth, was the site of the Jetavana monastery. It became an important place of pilgrimage, adorned with numerous shrines, stupas and monasteries. The stupas belong mostly to the Kushana period, while the temples are in the Gupta style. The remains date from the Mauryan era (third century BCE) to the twelfth century CE. One of the earliest stupas. Probably dating to the 3rd century BC contained relics of the Buddha. A colossal statue of the Buddha was also found here which is now preserved in the Indian Museum, Calcutta. The Emperor Ashoka visited Jetavana, and the Chinese pilgrim Hiuen- Tsang mentions two Ashokan pillars at Sravasti.

sections.heading: Dashavatar Temple
sections.content: Deogarh is situated on the right bank of the Betwa river, at the western end of the Lalitpur range of hills. It is of great antiquarian, epigraphical and archaeological importance and has been integral to the history of the Guptas, the Gurjara-Pratiharas, the Gondas, the Muslim rulers of Delhi, the Marathas and the British. It possesses the remains of a fine Vishnu temple dating to the Gupta era, and several Jain temples.The architecture and sculpture of these temples display a high level of craftsmanship. Dashavatar Temple is a fine Gupta temple dedicated to Lord Vishnu and is the earliest known Panchyatan temple in north India. The terraced basement above the high plinth is decorated with sculpted panels. The figures of Ganga and Yamuna adorn the carved doorway leading to the sanctum sanctorum. Three large carved panels along the side walls-the Gajendramoksha panel, the Nar Narayan Tapasya and the Anantshayi Vishnu-depict scenes from Vaishnava mythology. Only the lower portion remains of the spire, which was the most important part of the temple.

sections.heading: Uttar Pradesh- Monument- Jain Temples
sections.content: The 31 Jain temples are somewhat later in origin that the Vishnu temple, but are no less remarkable. They are situated inside the fort of Kanali on the hills overlooking the Betwa. The temples abound in panels depicting scenes from Jain mythology, Tirthankara images, votive pillars, votive tablets, Jain images visible from all sides and pillars carved with a thousand Jain figures.

sections.heading: Uttar Pradesh- Monument- Bhitargaon Temple
sections.content: Situated in Ghatampur tehsil, Bhitargaon is a unique architectural specimen  a brick temple with a shikara belonging to the Gupta period. Built of large bricks and set in mud mortar, the total height of the temple is 15.41m. Inside the temple only the sanctum or garbhagriha and the porch exist. The most remarked feature of the temple is its recessed plan. In contrast to the interior the exterior is decorated with carved brickwork and numerous terracotta panels of skilful workmanship. The importance of the Bhitargaon temple lies in the fact that it is the sole surviving record of this early phase of temple architecture in India.

sections.heading: Uttar Pradesh- Handicrafts- Stone inlay work work
sections.content: Pietra dura is Agra's fabled inlay work of precious stones like lapiz lazuli and machelite on marble. The mosaics formed by the inlay work range from beautiful floral patterns to free flowing flower and vine themes on table tops, bowls, wall hangings, etc. The best of pietra dura work featuring delicate and intricate mosaics in jewel like colours is made in Agra. Vrindavan is a centre of exquisite alabaster figures, fret work traceries and jaals.

sections.heading: Uttar Pradesh- Handicrafts- Embroidery
sections.content: Lucknow's craftswomen are known for their Chikankari. The name chikan seems to have been derived from the Persian word, either Chikan, Chikin or Chikeen. It means a kind of cloth wrought with needlework. A delicate and subtle embroidery, reminiscent of the shadow work of Isphahan in Persia, Chikankari's charm lies in the minuteness, evenness and sheer excellence of craft as well as the use of white embroidery on white cloth. Chief among the stitches are murree, lepchi, keelkangan, bakhia in which forms are outlined on the right side with minute stitches while the threads are concentrated on the wrong side, giving the motifs an opaque shadowy quality. The motifs of chikankari range from floral and vine themes to birds, animals and arabesques.

sections.heading: Uttar Pradesh- Handicrafts- Weaving
sections.content: Sari weaving is a cottage industry for millions of people around Varanasi. Most of the silk for the Banarasi saris comes from south India, mainly from Bangalore. Kinkhab is the art of using gold and silver thread on fine silk and cotton to create the rich brocades of Varanasi gold thread on a silver background creates the beautiful shimmering tissues. Breathtakingly beautiful, they are embellished with bird, animal and geometric patterns in the butidar and jaal style.Weavers known as karigars weave saris in workshops known as karkhanas. The design motifs of these brocades are intricate floral and foliage patterns, kalga and bel, and in sari pallaus and dupattas a string of upright leaves called jhalar.

sections.heading: Uttar Pradesh- Handicrafts- Carpet Weaving
sections.content: Varanasi and its neighboring areas are well known for carpet making. The Varanasi-Bhadohi-Mirzapur belt in Uttar Pradesh produces maximum number of carpets in the country. They have their own distinct designs such as the Taj Mahal, Kethariwala Jal, Jamabaz, Kandhari, etc. Embossed, sculpted carpets in the Chinese style are also produced in Mirzapur.

sections.heading: Uttar Pradesh- Handicrafts- Metal craft
sections.content: Moradabad in western Uttar Pradesh produces large quantities of metalware, specially brassware and it is famous for its coloured enamelling and intricate engraving. While engravings of the nakashi type are done on tinned surface, khudai is done on lac coated unpolished brass on which a pointed steel pencil is used to make the design later filled with lac of different hues. Today, apart from traditional vases, stools, etc. beautiful contemporary bowls, trays, and images of different deities are being made in Moradabad.

sections.heading: Woodwork
sections.content: Saharanpur is well-known for its carved and brass inlay furniture items and other artifacts. Sheesham, sal and dudhi wood are used to make well-finished screens, room dividers and furniture items featuring jaali or lattice work and brass inlay work in floral and geometric patterns. The furniture artifacts are attractive with an increasing amount of contemporary design input.

sections.heading: Pottery
sections.content: Khurja pottery has evolved a style of its own by raising the pattern with the use of thick slips into a light relief. The shades of the pottery are in warm autumnal colours like orange, brown, and a special light red. Floral designs in sky blue are worked against a white background. A speciality of Khurja is a type of long pitcher decorated in relief by a thick slip. Specialized glazed items like tableware for modern use are produced in Chinhat and Mausalia. A very special kind of earthenware peculiar to Nizamabada and Azamgarh districts of Uttar Pradesh is distinguished by its dark lustrous finish.

sections.heading: Uttar Pradesh- Handicrafts- Glass
sections.content: Ferozabad is a glass town where the entire community seems to be involved in making glassware. Originally only glass bangles were made here, but now all types of sophisticated glassware including tasteful tableware is produced.

sections.heading: Bharat Kala Bhawan- Varanasi
sections.content: Bharat Kala Bhavan located in the Banaras Hindu University has an outstanding collection of sculptures, paintings and textiles which began with the private collection of the eminent art historian Rai Krishnadasa. The sculpture collection includes terracotta and clay objects, stone and bronze and cast metal objects. Ancient terracotta varying from ritual icons to toys to utilitarian objects date to the Indus Valley civilisation, Mauryan, Sunga and Gupta periods. Among the stone sculpture are red sandstone reliefs from the second century BCE Buddhist stupa at Bharhut and rare images and statues from well known schools like Gandhara, which saw the synthesis of Greek and Indian styles and Mathura, a powerful art centre during the Kushana period. The large and impressive collection of textiles contain precious examples of Banaras silks and brocades, embroidered shawls from Kashmir and the rare Chamba rumal, onceused to wrap ceremonial gifts and offerings. They consist of rich embroidered pieces with designs and stories from the life of Krishna. Miniatures from almost all the schools of painting are represented here: Mughal, Rajasthani and Pahari.

sections.heading: Uttar Pradesh- Performing Art- Dance- Kathak
sections.content: Kathak is the major classical dance form of northern India. There are three main gharanas, or schools of kathak; Jaipur, Lucknow, and the Benares. Each has a slight difference in interpretation and repertoire. The word kathak means "to tell a story". It is derived from the dance dramas of ancient India. It started its journey from the courts of Emperors and Nawabs of the then Awadh and has traversed a path that was full of turmoil to reach where it is i.e. in the hearts of the masses. Kathak has the monopoly of courtesans and consorts in its early phase. This dance form was primarily developed for the amusement of royals that wanted a slight break from the pure classical dances. Therefore a dance form was born that was semi-classical in nature and was based on the Persian, Awadhi and Urdu poetry. This dance form saw volatile changes with the downfall of royalty in India. The dance is primarily an abstract exploration of rhythm and movement. Kathak demands the highest standards of training, intelligence, and most important, civility.

sections.heading: Uttar Pradesh- Fairs & Festivals- Ganga Dusshera
sections.content: Ganga has been considered by Hindus as a holy river for time immemorable and being worshipped. Various pilgrimages are situated along this river, which are the hubs of fairs, festivities and worship by millions of Hindus every year. Ten days in the month of Jyeshtha (June) Ganga Dussehra is celebrated at Rishikesh, Haridwar, Garhmukteshwar, Prayag and Varanasi. Devotees take a holy dip in the Ganga, worship it, collect the clay from the banks/ ghats and take it home. Thousands of lamps are floated into the Ganga after aarti at the dusk. Lucknow, the capital of Uttar Pradesh situated along the banks of the river Gomti, rose to prominence as the centre of the Nawabs of Avadh. Historically reputed as a city of culture, it is famous for its gharana of music, Kathak dance and chikankari work (shadow work embroidery) and the huge mausoleums of thenawabs, and the ruins of the Residency stand witness to one of the most remarkable episodes in the Revolt of 1857. During Akbars reign (1556-1605), Oudh, as Lucknow was then called, flourished under imperial patronage. In early eighteenth century, the Mughal Emperor Muhammad Shah, appointed Nawab Sadat Khan Burhan-ul-Mulk as the Governor of Oudh beginning the reign of the Nawabs over Oudh, which continued till the close of the eighteenth Century. It was under Asaf-ud-Daulah, the fourth Nawab that Lucknow prospered and grew into a sophisticated and picturesque city with palaces, gardens and imposing architectural monuments. The Nawabs patronage of music and arts attracted poets, artists, and musicians to Lucknow in large numbers. During these eventful years, Lucknow became one of the most celebrated centers of opulence, dance, poetry and scholarship.
